findings.body:
Removing `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and posting directly to the caller-supplied `url` enables server-side request forgery. A customer- or attacker-controlled endpoint can make this runner POST event payloads to cloud metadata (`169.254.169.254`), localhost, or internal RFC1918 hosts; `urllib.request.urlopen` also follows redirects by default, which widens the blast radius.

Restore an egress allow policy before merge: HTTPS-only, resolve and block private/link-local/metadata IPs (including after redirects), and keep a configurable allowlist or equivalent safe-customer-endpoint validator. Do not ship open `urlopen` on untrusted URLs.

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change removes the only host allowlist on webhook delivery and turns `deliver()` into an open SSRF primitive.

## Analysis

`webhooks.py` previously restricted outbound POSTs to `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`hooks.internal.example`). The PR deletes that check and posts to whatever `url` the caller supplies, with only a comment noting customer endpoints.

Any attacker-controlled or loosely validated customer URL can now target:
- cloud metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`)
- localhost / link-local / RFC1918 admin panels
- internal service mesh hosts
- non-HTTP schemes `urllib` may still open

`urllib.request.urlopen` also follows redirects by default, so even a future hostname allowlist is insufficient without post-redirect re-validation and private-IP blocking.

Supporting customer webhooks is a product need; it requires an explicit egress policy (HTTPS-only, DNS rebinding-safe IP checks, block list for link-local/metadata/private ranges, redirect handling, size/time limits), not deletion of the gate.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The patch removes ALLOWED_HOSTS and the hostname check that previously rejected non-allowlisted webhook URLs, so deliver() now POSTs via urllib.request.urlopen to any caller-supplied url with no egress controls—enabling SSRF to metadata/internal hosts as claimed.
